questions.stem: A 72 year old man has a 2 day history of high fever, rigors and a cough productive of rust-coloured sputum. He has cold sores on his upper lip. His temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There is bronchial breathing at the right base. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Dense right lower lobe consolidation: lobar pneumonia.

questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Rust-coloured sputum, high fever, lobar consolidation and herpes labialis are the classic picture of pneumococcal pneumonia, the commonest cause of CAP. Klebsiella gives redcurrant jelly sputum instead.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?

clues: bronchial breathing at the right base
steps.x: Rust sputum + lobar consolidation + herpes labialis = pneumococcus.

elim: Linked to COPD exacerbations; does not cause rust-coloured sputum with herpes labialis.
Redcurrant jelly sputum in alcohol use or diabetes, usually upper lobe.
Travel history, confusion, hyponatraemia and bi-basal change; none here.
Dry cough, mild chest signs and diffuse infiltrates, not lobar consolidation.

steps.x: E: Streptococcus pneumoniae. Strep. pneumoniae is the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with COPD has a 4 day history of increased breathlessness, fever and a cough productive of green sputum. She uses salbutamol and tiotropium inhalers. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 136/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. There are coarse crackles at the left base. Sputum Gram stain shows Gram-negative coccobacilli.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: H. influenzae is a Gram-negative coccobacillus and the classic pneumonia organism in COPD. Pneumococcus is common too but is Gram-positive.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?
COPD plus Gram-negative coccobacilli points to one organism.

elim: Gram-negative rod, not a coccobacillus; associated with alcohol and diabetes.
A fungus in HIV with CD4 <200; not seen on Gram stain.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters, typically after influenza.
Gram-positive diplococci.

steps.x: A: Haemophilus influenzae. Gram-negative coccobacillus in COPD = Haemophilus influenzae.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman is on the orthopaedic ward five days after a hip hemiarthroplasty performed under spinal anaesthesia. She develops a fever, breathlessness and a new cough productive of purulent sputum. She has had no vomiting or choking episodes. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. There are crackles at the left base.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pneumonia starting 48 hours or more after admission is hospital-acquired (S. aureus, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, H. influenzae). VAP needs 48 hours after intubation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Timing from admission defines CAP vs HAP; intubation defines VAP.

elim: No vomiting, choking or swallowing problem is described.
Purulent sputum and hospital onset point to a typical bacterial HAP.
Symptoms began more than 48 hours after admission.
She was never intubated (spinal anaesthetic).

steps.x: D: Hospital-acquired pneumonia. Onset at least 48 hours after admission = HAP.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man was admitted 30 hours ago for observation after a minor head injury; his CT head was normal. He now has a fever, right-sided pleuritic pain and a cough productive of yellow sputum, which his wife says started the evening before admission. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. There are crackles at the right base.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pneumonia presenting within 48 hours of admission is community-acquired, so the likely organism is still Strep. pneumoniae. HAP needs onset at 48 hours or later.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Under 48 hours since admission, and symptoms began at home.

elim: He has not had reduced consciousness, vomiting or a swallowing problem.
Productive cough and focal signs suggest typical bacterial infection.
HAP starts at least 48 hours after admission; this began within 48 hours.
He has not been intubated.

steps.x: C: Community-acquired pneumonia. Within 48 hours of admission counts as CAP.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has been intubated and ventilated on the intensive care unit for four days after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Over 24 hours her FiO2 requirement has risen from 0.3 to 0.55 and suction brings up thick yellow secretions. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 108/64 mmHg. Her chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: At least 48 hours after intubation, fever, rising oxygen needs, purulent secretions and a new infiltrate define VAP. ARDS is bilateral and not purulent.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
These are the four VAP criteria: pyrexia, rising O2 needs, purulent secretions, new infiltrate.

elim: Gives bilateral infiltrates without purulent secretions or a focal new infiltrate.
Chemical injury within hours of aspiration, not after four days of ventilation with purulent secretions.
Bilateral, no fever or purulent secretions.
Would not cause purulent secretions or a new consolidation with fever.

steps.x: E: Ventilator-associated pneumonia. Pneumonia at least 48 hours after intubation = VAP.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has been ventilated on intensive care for 10 days after a road traffic collision. He has had two courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics. He develops a new fever, a rising oxygen requirement and green purulent endotracheal secretions. Endotracheal aspirate culture grows an oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Late VAP after repeated antibiotics is caused by multi-drug resistant organisms; an oxidase-positive non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod is Pseudomonas.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?

clues: ventilated on intensive care for 10 days
steps.x: Long ventilation plus prior antibiotics selects resistant Gram-negatives.

elim: Bird exposure in the community; not a VAP organism.
A coccobacillus, and not the typical multi-drug resistant VAP organism.
Has no cell wall, so it does not Gram stain; a community atypical.
Gram-positive diplococcus causing CAP.

steps.x: D: Pseudomonas aeruginosa. VAP organisms: Pseudomonas, MSSA/MRSA and other Gram-negatives.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man with alcohol dependence was found unresponsive by his partner after a heavy night of drinking, having vomited. Three days later he has a fever and a cough productive of foul-smelling sputum. He has poor dentition. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There are coarse crackles at the right base.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Reduced consciousness with vomiting, alcohol and poor oral hygiene, then foul sputum and right basal crackles, is aspiration pneumonia with anaerobes. TB is chronic and upper lobe.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Risk factors for aspiration plus foul sputum in a dependent zone.

elim: Chronic daily sputum over years, not an acute illness after vomiting.
Travel, confusion, myalgia and hyponatraemia; sputum is not foul.
HIV with CD4 <200, dry cough and exertional desaturation.
Weeks of cough, weight loss, night sweats and upper lobe disease.

steps.x: A: Aspiration pneumonia. Foul sputum + aspiration risk + right lower zone = aspiration pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman was treated for aspiration pneumonia three weeks ago after a middle cerebral artery stroke left her with dysphagia. She now has a swinging fever, night sweats and a cough producing large amounts of foul-smelling sputum. Her temperature is 38.9°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. Her chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level in the right lower zone.

questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: A thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level and copious foul sputum after aspiration is a lung abscess. Empyema is in the pleural space, not the lung.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely complication?
Aspiration pneumonia can liquefy into an abscess cavity.

elim: Possible cavitating mass, but swinging fever and foul sputum after aspiration point to infection.
Pus in the pleural space gives a pleural collection, not a cavity within the lung.
Sudden breathlessness with absent lung markings, not a cavity with fever.
Usually upper lobe, without an aspiration history or foul sputum.

steps.x: C: Lung abscess. Lung abscess is the classic complication of aspiration pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has a 10 day history of a dry cough, headache, sore throat and tiredness, but has carried on working. He now looks pale and slightly jaundiced. His temperature is 37.9°C and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. There are only a few scattered crackles, but a chest X-ray shows diffuse patchy infiltrates in both lungs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: A young adult with a dry cough, mild signs but diffuse infiltrates, haemolytic anaemia and deranged LFTs has Mycoplasma (cold autoimmune haemolysis). Legionella causes hyponatraemia, not haemolysis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?
Walking pneumonia with signs of haemolysis.

elim: Needs contact with birds.
Severe illness with redcurrant jelly sputum in alcohol use or diabetes.
Travel, confusion and hyponatraemia; does not cause haemolysis.
Severe post-influenza illness with cavitating lesions.

steps.x: D: Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Mycoplasma: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, abnormal LFTs, erythema multiforme.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man returned five days ago from a week-long business conference at a large hotel. He has fever, muscle aches, headache, diarrhoea and a cough. He is disorientated in time. His temperature is 39.7°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. There are crackles at both lung bases.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his blood tests?
questions.e: Hotel stay, high fever, myalgia, headache, confusion and bi-basal crackles suggest Legionella, which classically causes hyponatraemia. Cold agglutinins belong to Mycoplasma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on his blood tests?

clues: business conference at a large hotel
steps.x: Travel + flu-like illness + confusion = Legionella.

elim: Suggests parasitic or eosinophilic lung disease, not Legionella.
Seen with malignancy or sarcoidosis, not this travel-associated pneumonia.
Not a feature of Legionella; neutrophilia is more likely.
Points to Mycoplasma, which causes a milder illness without confusion.

steps.x: C: Hyponatraemia. Legionella's signature blood result is a low sodium.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman who breeds parrots at home has a 1 week history of fever, headache, muscle aches and a dry cough. Several of her birds have recently been unwell. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows patchy consolidation in the left lower zone.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: A flu-like atypical pneumonia in someone with sick pet birds is psittacosis (Chlamydia psittaci). Mycoplasma has no bird link.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?

clues: muscle aches and a dry cough
steps.x: Bird contact names the organism.

elim: Associated with COPD; no link to birds.
Linked to travel and water systems, not birds.
Also flu-like, but the bird contact is the decisive clue.
Productive rust-coloured sputum and lobar consolidation.

steps.x: A: Chlamydia psittaci. Birds + flu-like pneumonia = Chlamydia psittaci.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has a 4 day history of fever and a cough productive of thick, blood-stained, jelly-like sputum. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 114 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. There is bronchial breathing in the right upper zone.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on sputum Gram stain?
questions.e: Redcurrant jelly sputum and upper lobe disease in a diabetic is Klebsiella pneumoniae, a Gram-negative rod. Pneumococcus is a Gram-positive diplococcus.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on sputum Gram stain?
Redcurrant jelly sputum in a diabetic = Klebsiella.

elim: H. influenzae, linked to COPD.
Moraxella or Neisseria, not the redcurrant jelly organism.
S. aureus after influenza, with cavitation.
Strep. pneumoniae, which gives rust-coloured sputum.

steps.x: C: Gram-negative rods. Klebsiella is a Gram-negative rod.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman had laboratory-confirmed influenza A two weeks ago and was recovering. Over the past 2 days she has developed a high fever, a cough productive of purulent sputum and worsening breathlessness. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
questions.e: Severe pneumonia after influenza with Gram-positive cocci in clusters is S. aureus, which classically forms cavitating lesions. Ground-glass change is PCP.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
Post-influenza + Gram-positive cocci in clusters = S. aureus.

elim: Suggests sarcoidosis or lymphoma.
Typical of PCP in HIV.
Seen with an obstructing lesion or mucus plug, not this organism.
A chronic process, e.g. old TB.

steps.x: E: Widespread cavitating lesions. S. aureus pneumonia cavitates.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has a 4 week history of a non-productive cough, fevers and breathlessness that is worst on stairs. He has lost 5 kg and has oral candidiasis. His oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air at rest, falling to 88% after a short walk. A CT chest shows bilateral ground-glass opacities.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: HIV with CD4 below 200, a dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, exercise desaturation and ground-glass opacities on CT is PCP. TB cavitates and is usually upper lobe.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: falling to 88% after a short walk
steps.x: Exercise desaturation and ground glass in advanced HIV.

elim: Causes nodules and haemoptysis, with skin or mucosal lesions.
A mild illness of young, immunocompetent adults; it does not explain oral candidiasis and weight loss.
Acute productive cough with lobar consolidation.
Productive cough, often cavitating upper lobe disease rather than diffuse ground glass.

steps.x: D: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. CD4 <200 + exercise desaturation + ground glass = PCP.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is on day 7 of treatment for right lower lobe pneumonia. His fever settled but has returned, spiking each evening. There is stony dullness and reduced breath sounds at the right base. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources). A diagnostic pleural aspirate is cloudy.

visual.title: Chest X-ray, day 7
visual.caption: Right pleural effusion with a meniscus.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A swinging fever returning during pneumonia treatment, a basal effusion and cloudy fluid with pH below 7.2 and low glucose is empyema. A heart failure transudate has normal pH.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: fever settled but has returned, spiking each evening
stony dullness and reduced breath sounds
steps.x: Recurrent swinging fever despite antibiotics plus an effusion.

elim: Needs trauma or bleeding; fluid is blood-stained, not low pH and cloudy.
Slow onset with weight loss; pH is rarely this low with fever.
Bilateral, clear fluid with normal pH and glucose.
Weeks of symptoms and lymphocytic fluid; not a swinging fever after pneumonia.

steps.x: A: Empyema. Pleural pH <7.2 in pneumonia = empyema: drain it.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is admitted with a 3 day history of cough and fever. He is alert and orientated. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. His blood tests are shown.
questions.q: Which result is the most important marker of a poor prognosis?
questions.e: Urea above 7 mmol/L is a poor prognostic marker in CAP and scores a point on CURB-65, reflecting renal hypoperfusion. CRP and white cell count are not in the score.

steps.x: The question asks: Which result is the most important marker of a poor prognosis?
Which of these results is in CURB-65?

elim: Shows inflammation but is not part of the CURB-65 prognostic score.
Only mildly low and not a prognostic marker in CAP.
Mild hyponatraemia; not a CURB-65 criterion.
Expected in bacterial pneumonia; not a CURB-65 criterion.

steps.x: D: Urea 11.4 mmol/L. Urea >7 mmol/L predicts mortality in CAP.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a 3 day history of fever and a productive cough. His abbreviated mental test score is 10/10. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 31 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There are crackles at the right base and a chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of his CURB-65 score?
o: Score 1: low severity, treat in the community
Score 2: moderate severity, consider hospital admission
questions.e: Urea above 7 and respiratory rate of 30 or more give 2 points: moderate severity, consider admission. AMTS 10, BP 134/82 and age 52 score nothing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of his CURB-65 score?
Count each criterion: C, U, R, B, 65.

elim: Both urea and respiratory rate score, so it is higher than 1.
He is not confused, hypotensive or 65 or over.
Only two criteria are met.
Overcounts; only urea and respiratory rate score.

steps.x: B: Score 2: moderate severity, consider hospital admission. CURB-65 of 2 = moderate: consider hospital admission.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She has a cough productive of green sputum and is breathless at rest. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. Blood has been sent for U&Es.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: In pneumonia an ABG is needed when oxygen saturation is below 92% to assess oxygenation and ventilation. U&Es are already sent for the urea in CURB-65.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

clues: Blood has been sent for U&Es
steps.x: Saturation is below the 92% threshold.

elim: Used for long-term oxygen planning in chronic disease, not acute pneumonia.
Consolidation and sputum explain her hypoxia; no PE features.
Used in asthma, not to assess oxygenation in pneumonia.
Not done in an acutely unwell, hypoxic patient.

steps.x: B: Arterial blood gas. SpO2 <92% in pneumonia = do an ABG.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man presents to the emergency department with a 3 day history of fever, a cough productive of green sputum and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There is dullness to percussion and bronchial breathing at the right base.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Chest X-ray showing consolidation is the key first investigation for pneumonia. CTPA would be for PE.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

clues: dullness to percussion and bronchial breathing
steps.x: Signs of consolidation: image it first.

elim: Invasive; reserved for PCP, non-resolving pneumonia or suspected obstruction.
Not first-line; used if the X-ray is unclear or complications are suspected.
For pulmonary embolism; productive cough and focal signs point to pneumonia.
Identifies the organism later but does not confirm consolidation.

steps.x: B: Chest X-ray. Chest X-ray confirms pneumonia by showing consolidation.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman is admitted with a 2 day history of high fever and a cough productive of rust-coloured sputum. She was given one dose of amoxicillin by her GP yesterday, so sputum culture may be negative. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows right middle lobe consolidation.
questions.q: Which test is most likely to identify the causative organism?
questions.e: Rust-coloured sputum with lobar consolidation suggests Strep. pneumoniae, diagnosed with a urinary antigen test, which stays positive after antibiotics are started. Serology is for Mycoplasma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which test is most likely to identify the causative organism?
Classic pneumococcal picture; culture may be spoiled by antibiotics.

elim: Used for Mycoplasma; the picture here is typical lobar pneumonia.
Used for PCP in HIV.
For latent TB, not acute pneumonia.
Would not identify the bacterial cause of lobar pneumonia.

steps.x: D: Pneumococcal urinary antigen. Strep. pneumoniae: urinary antigen test.

questions.stem: A 20 year old student has a 2 week history of a dry cough, headache and tiredness. She has kept going to lectures. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 86 bpm, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Chest signs are minimal, but her chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates. Several students in her halls have similar symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the gold-standard investigation to confirm the most likely organism?
questions.e: A young adult with walking pneumonia (dry cough, mild signs, diffuse infiltrates) in a closed community suggests Mycoplasma, confirmed by blood serology. BAL is the PCP test.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the gold-standard investigation to confirm the most likely organism?
Mild illness, diffuse infiltrates, young adult = Mycoplasma.

elim: Rarely positive and Mycoplasma does not grow on standard culture.
Gold standard for PCP in HIV, not Mycoplasma.
Would be for travel-associated pneumonia with confusion and hyponatraemia.
Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall so it does not Gram stain.

steps.x: B: Blood serology. Mycoplasma: blood serology is the gold standard.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with HIV has a 3 week history of a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion. Her CD4 count is 140 cells/µL. Her oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air at rest and falls to 87% on walking. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar interstitial shadowing. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage is performed.
questions.q: Which stain is most likely to show the organism?
questions.e: PCP is confirmed by bronchoscopy with BAL, and the cysts are best stained with methenamine silver. Ziehl-Neelsen is for TB.

steps.x: The question asks: Which stain is most likely to show the organism?
Classic PCP; now pick the stain for the BAL sample.

elim: A fluorescent stain for mycobacteria.
Pneumocystis is a fungus and is not seen on Gram stain.
Shows Cryptococcus in CSF.
Shows acid-fast bacilli in TB.

steps.x: D: Methenamine silver stain. PCP: BAL stained with methenamine silver.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man is on day 5 of oral antibiotics for left lower lobe pneumonia. He has a recurrent swinging fever. There is dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds at the left base. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. His chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A swinging fever despite antibiotics with a basal effusion suggests empyema; the first-line test is a pleural aspirate to check pH (below 7.2 means empyema).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

clues: dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds at the left base
steps.x: Suspected empyema: sample the fluid.

elim: For non-resolving pneumonia or suspected obstruction; the effusion must be sampled first.
Swinging fever and an effusion after pneumonia suggest infection, not PE.
Follow-up after recovery; he is unwell now.
Will not show whether the pleural fluid is infected.

steps.x: C: Diagnostic pleural aspirate. Empyema: first-line investigation is pleural aspirate.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man was admitted six days ago with decompensated heart failure. He now has a fever and a cough productive of purulent sputum. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 106 bpm, BP 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows new right lower zone consolidation. The team plan to start intravenous antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting antibiotics?
o: Blood cultures and a sputum sample
questions.e: In hospital-acquired pneumonia, peripheral blood cultures and lower respiratory tract samples should be taken before antibiotics so treatment can be targeted. Legionella antigen is for CAP with travel.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting antibiotics?
Onset after 48 hours = HAP; culture before treating.

elim: Fever, purulent sputum and consolidation point to pneumonia.
Assesses heart failure but does not guide antibiotics.
No travel or atypical features; HAP organisms are the concern.
Does not identify the organism or its sensitivities.

steps.x: A: Blood cultures and a sputum sample. HAP: blood cultures and lower respiratory samples before antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has been ventilated on intensive care for three days after a cardiac arrest. She develops a temperature of 38.7°C, an increasing oxygen requirement and purulent secretions on suctioning. A chest X-ray shows a new right lower zone infiltrate. The team want to identify the organism before starting antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate microbiological investigation?
questions.e: VAP is investigated with an endotracheal aspirate culture, which samples the lower airway through the tube. Pneumococcal antigen is a CAP test.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate microbiological investigation?

clues: ventilated on intensive care for three days
steps.x: Over 48 hours ventilated with the four VAP features.

elim: Too invasive as a first sample.
Detects viruses in the upper airway, not the VAP organism.
Used for CAP; VAP organisms are resistant Gram-negatives and S. aureus.
Samples the throat, not the lower respiratory tract.

steps.x: B: Endotracheal aspirate culture. VAP: send an endotracheal aspirate for culture.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man is brought in by ambulance with a 3 day history of cough and fever. He is drowsy and struggling to breathe. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82% breathing air. There is bronchial breathing at the left base.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask
questions.e: In an acutely unwell, distressed patient the first step is ABC, so give high-flow oxygen for saturation of 82%, then start Sepsis Six with IV antibiotics. Investigations wait.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
He is peri-arrest: ABC first.

elim: Important, but oxygen comes first in a distressed hypoxic patient.
Investigation comes after stabilising airway and breathing.
Needed urgently, but breathing is treated first under ABC.
Identifies organisms later; not an emergency step.

steps.x: C: High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask. ABC before investigation in an acutely unwell patient.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman sees her GP with a 2 day history of fever and a cough productive of yellow sputum. She is alert and orientated and has no drug allergies. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. There are crackles at the left base.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Admit for intravenous co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin
Oral amoxicillin and clarithromycin with admission
Oral amoxicillin for 7 days with review at 48 hours
questions.e: She scores 0 on CURB-65 (low severity), so treat at home with oral amoxicillin for 7 days and review at 48 hours. Dual therapy and admission are for a score of 2.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Score each criterion: none is met.

elim: For CURB-65 of 3 or more or sepsis.
She has clinical pneumonia and needs antibiotics.
For CURB-65 of 2 (moderate).
Too broad and too long for low-severity CAP.

steps.x: D: Oral amoxicillin for 7 days with review at 48 hours. CURB-65 0-1: home with amoxicillin, review at 48 hours.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman is brought in from a care home with pneumonia. Her abbreviated mental test score is 5/10. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. She has no drug allergies. Oxygen and blood cultures have been given and taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: She scores 5 on CURB-65 and is septic, so she needs IV co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin in a high-dependency setting as part of Sepsis Six. Oral dual therapy is for a score of 2.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
Score of 5 and septic: severe CAP.

elim: VAP regimen with MRSA cover; she has severe CAP.
For low-severity CAP (CURB-65 0-1).
For moderate CAP (CURB-65 2).
Penicillin-allergy option for low-severity CAP.

steps.x: A: Intravenous co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin. CURB-65 3 or more: IV co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin, high-dependency care.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman was admitted five days ago with a fractured neck of femur. She develops a fever, a cough productive of purulent sputum and new left lower zone consolidation on chest X-ray. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 120/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. She has no drug allergies and her MRSA screen is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Pneumonia five days after admission is HAP, treated with IV piperacillin-tazobactam (or co-amoxiclav; meropenem if severe) to cover Gram-negatives and S. aureus. Amoxicillin is for CAP.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
HAP needs broader cover than CAP.

elim: Too narrow; does not cover HAP Gram-negatives like Pseudomonas and Klebsiella.
MRSA cover only, with no Gram-negative cover; her MRSA screen is negative.
First-line for low-severity CAP, not HAP.
CAP option for penicillin allergy.

steps.x: B: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam. HAP: IV piperacillin-tazobactam.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has been intubated on intensive care for six days after a perforated bowel. He develops fever, purulent endotracheal secretions, a rising oxygen requirement and a new infiltrate on chest X-ray. His admission screen grew MRSA from his nose. An endotracheal aspirate has been sent.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: VAP is treated first-line with piperacillin-tazobactam, adding vancomycin for MRSA cover when MRSA is a risk, as here. Pip-taz alone misses MRSA.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

clues: intubated on intensive care for six days
steps.x: VAP plus known MRSA carriage.

elim: Regimen for severe CAP; does not cover Pseudomonas or MRSA.
Covers Pseudomonas but not MRSA, which he carries.
Low-severity CAP only.
Low-severity CAP with penicillin allergy.

steps.x: C: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin. VAP: pip-taz, plus vancomycin if MRSA risk.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with COPD is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and a CURB-65 score of 2. He has no wheeze and his usual breathlessness is unchanged. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. He has been started on oral amoxicillin and clarithromycin.
questions.q: Which additional treatment is most appropriate?
questions.e: In pneumonia with COPD, give oral corticosteroids even when there is no evidence of a COPD exacerbation. NIV is only for hypercapnic failure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which additional treatment is most appropriate?
Pneumonia in a COPD patient, even without an exacerbation.

elim: For severe bronchospasm not responding to nebulisers; he has no wheeze.
Prophylaxis for frequent COPD exacerbations, not acute pneumonia.
For hypercapnic respiratory failure, which is not described.
Maintenance bronchodilator, not an addition for pneumonia.

steps.x: D: Oral prednisolone. Pneumonia + COPD: add oral steroids.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day was treated in hospital for right lower lobe pneumonia. Two weeks later at follow-up he feels completely well, with no cough, fever or weight loss. His chest is clear and his oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Repeat chest X-ray 6 weeks after clinical resolution
questions.e: All pneumonia cases have a repeat chest X-ray 6 weeks after clinical resolution to confirm clearance and exclude an underlying lesion, especially in smokers.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
Recovered pneumonia in a smoker: check the lung has cleared.

elim: Not indicated without persisting X-ray changes or red flags.
Consolidation takes weeks to clear; imaging now would be premature.
Not a routine follow-up test after pneumonia.
He has no red flags; the follow-up X-ray decides.

steps.x: C: Repeat chest X-ray 6 weeks after clinical resolution. Repeat CXR 6 weeks after clinical resolution.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman takes simvastatin 40 mg daily. She is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia, CURB-65 score 2, and started on amoxicillin and clarithromycin. Her simvastatin was not stopped. On day 4 she has aching, tender thigh muscles and dark urine. Her temperature is 37.2°C and her chest is improving.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her muscle symptoms?
o: Clarithromycin inhibition of CYP3A4 raising plasma simvastatin levels
questions.e: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, raising plasma statin levels and causing myopathy or rhabdomyolysis, so statins are held while it is given.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her muscle symptoms?

clues: aching, tender thigh muscles and dark urine
steps.x: A macrolide started on top of a statin, then myopathy.

elim: Amoxicillin does not interact with statins or commonly cause myositis.
She has not been given steroids, and steroid myopathy is proximal weakness without a high CK.
Potassium is normal.
Fever has settled and the timing follows the new drug.

steps.x: B: Clarithromycin inhibition of CYP3A4 raising plasma simvastatin levels. Hold statins while giving clarithromycin.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has right lower lobe pneumonia. His oxygen saturation is 88% breathing air and rises only to 91% on 40% oxygen. A chest X-ray shows dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms. An arterial blood gas is taken breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
o: Exudate filling alveoli so blood perfuses unventilated lung
questions.e: Inflammatory exudate fills the alveoli, causing consolidation; blood flowing past unventilated alveoli (shunt) causes hypoxaemia that responds poorly to oxygen. Hypoventilation would raise pCO2.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
Hypoxia that barely improves with oxygen means shunt.

elim: Would cause a raised pCO2; his pCO2 is low.
No fibrosis; the X-ray shows acute consolidation.
Haemoglobin is normal, and this does not lower pO2.
No cardiac defect; the shunt is within the consolidated lung.

steps.x: C: Exudate filling alveoli so blood perfuses unventilated lung. Exudate in alveoli impairs gas exchange.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with Parkinson's disease has been fed through a nasogastric tube for a week because of an unsafe swallow. He develops a fever and a cough productive of foul-smelling sputum. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. His chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: NG feeding and an unsafe swallow cause aspiration into the dependent right lower lobe; foul sputum reflects mixed anaerobic oral flora.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause?
Aspiration risk and foul sputum.

elim: Needs travel or water exposure; sputum is not foul.
Chronic, upper lobe, not foul sputum after NG feeding.
Dry cough with diffuse infiltrates in younger patients.
HIV with CD4 <200, dry cough, ground glass.

steps.x: B: Mixed oral anaerobic flora. Aspiration pneumonia: mixed anaerobes, right lower lobe.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman was started on amoxicillin by her GP for a chest infection five days ago. She still has a dry cough and headache but feels well enough to work. Her oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air. Her chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral interstitial shadowing that looks worse than her chest sounds. Serology confirms Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
questions.q: Which best explains why amoxicillin has not worked?
o: Amoxicillin is poorly absorbed when taken orally
The organism has altered penicillin-binding proteins
The organism lacks a cell wall
questions.e: Atypical organisms like Mycoplasma have no typical bacterial cell wall, so beta-lactams such as amoxicillin, which act on cell wall synthesis, cannot work; a macrolide or doxycycline is needed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains why amoxicillin has not worked?

clues: looks worse than her chest sounds
steps.x: Walking pneumonia not responding to a beta-lactam.

elim: Oral amoxicillin is well absorbed.
The mechanism of penicillin-resistant pneumococcus, not Mycoplasma.
Mycoplasma is a bacterium.
Mycoplasma has no target for beta-lactams in the first place.

steps.x: D: The organism lacks a cell wall. Atypical = no cell wall = beta-lactams fail.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man with untreated HIV has a 3 week history of a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion. His CD4 count is 60 cells/µL. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air, falling to 85% on exercise. A CT chest shows diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities, without lobar consolidation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the ground-glass appearance?
o: Diffuse interstitial pneumonitis with alveoli filled by organisms and exudate
Pulmonary oedema from left ventricular failure
questions.e: PCP causes a diffuse interstitial pneumonitis in which alveoli fill with organisms and foamy exudate rather than dense bacterial consolidation, giving partial filling and ground-glass change.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for the ground-glass appearance?

clues: diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities, without lobar consolidation
steps.x: PCP in advanced HIV: why ground glass and not consolidation?

elim: Seen in TB, giving nodules and cavities.
Chronic and gives reticulation and honeycombing.
Typical bacterial pneumonia, e.g. pneumococcus; not ground glass.
No cardiac history; the immunosuppression explains it.

steps.x: B: Diffuse interstitial pneumonitis with alveoli filled by organisms and exudate. PCP: partial alveolar filling = ground glass.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. Her abbreviated mental test score is 9/10. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Her urea is 13.2 mmol/L (2.5–7.8). The registrar explains why urea is part of the CURB-65 score.
questions.q: Which best explains why a raised urea predicts mortality in pneumonia?
o: It indicates hepatic involvement by the infection
It indicates the organism is atypical
It measures the extent of lung consolidation
It reflects renal impairment from hypoperfusion and decompensation
questions.e: CURB-65 captures physiological decompensation, renal impairment and frailty; a high urea reflects dehydration and renal hypoperfusion from sepsis, and the score guides how intensively to treat.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains why a raised urea predicts mortality in pneumonia?

clues: why urea is part of the CURB-65 score
steps.x: Think what urea measures physiologically.

elim: Urea reflects kidney function and hydration, not the liver.
Urea does not distinguish organisms.
Consolidation is assessed on X-ray.
Urea has no link to antibiotic resistance.

steps.x: E: It reflects renal impairment from hypoperfusion and decompensation. Urea >7 = renal hypoperfusion = higher mortality.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman is on day 9 of treatment for left lower lobe pneumonia. Her chest X-ray on admission showed a small left pleural effusion. She now has a recurrent swinging fever and the effusion has enlarged. A pleural aspirate is turbid with a pH of 7.0 and low glucose.
questions.q: Which is the most likely process that has occurred?
o: Raised hydrostatic pressure from heart failure
Secondary infection of a parapneumonic effusion
questions.e: Empyema develops when a parapneumonic effusion becomes secondarily infected; bacterial metabolism and anaerobic glycolysis lower the pH below 7.2 and use up glucose.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely process that has occurred?

clues: turbid with a pH of 7.0 and low glucose
steps.x: An effusion next to pneumonia that has turned infected.

elim: Fluid would be blood-stained; fever and low pH point to infection.
Malignant effusions develop slowly without swinging fever.
Gives a transudate with normal pH.
Possible after abdominal surgery, but here the effusion followed pneumonia.

steps.x: D: Secondary infection of a parapneumonic effusion. Empyema = infected parapneumonic effusion, pH <7.2.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a 2 day history of high fever, rigors and right-sided pleuritic pain. He coughs up rust-coloured sputum. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 120/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. There is bronchial breathing over the right upper zone. Sputum shows numerous neutrophils and Gram-positive diplococci.
questions.q: Which best explains the colour of his sputum?
o: Production of a red pigment by the organism
Red cells leaking into alveoli with a strong neutrophil response
questions.e: Strep. pneumoniae causes lobar consolidation with a robust neutrophilic response; red cells leak into the alveolar exudate and give rust-coloured sputum.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains the colour of his sputum?
Pneumococcal lobar pneumonia: what fills the alveoli?

elim: Pneumococcus causes lobar consolidation, not cavitation.
Haemolysis is a Mycoplasma feature and does not colour sputum.
No chronic sputum history.
Pneumococcus does not make pigment.

steps.x: E: Red cells leaking into alveoli with a strong neutrophil response. Rust sputum = red cells in a neutrophil-rich alveolar exudate.
